newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh to set up share depository to curb fraud.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh to set up share depository to curb fraud.

text.p: Bangladesh's Securities and Exchange Commission is setting up a central depository system to curb forged share certificates and to modernise trading on the growing bourse, SEC officials said.
"This will prevent forgery in the capital market, ensure transparency and protect the interest of investors," SEC Chairman Haroonur Rashid told Reuters on Friday.

Brokers said the SEC move had been prompted by the seizure of forged share certificates of some blue chips. The system would provide all necessary services and facilities to investors on listed companies, they said.
SEC officials and brokers said that in the planned system investors' share certificates would be preserved in a computer database to be installed in the stock exchange.
Investors would not need to exchange the share certificates in person, unlike the present system where they first take possession of the documents, then have them endorsed by the companies.

The SEC has already formed a six-member committee to work out the framework of the system. The panel will hold its first meeting on Sunday and was expected to submit an initial report by the end of this month, SEC officials said.
"This is only the first step," Rashid said. "It may take one to two years' time. It will need to amend company laws and computerisation (of the Dhaka Stock Exchange)," he said.
A.K.M. Sahabub Alam, an SEC member said the formation of the central depository system (CDS) was necessary to cater to the needs of the fast-growing capital market in the country.
"The introduction of CDS will ensure proper transfer of share certificates traded on the floor," Alam said.
Former Dhaka stock exchange chairman Khurshid Alam welcomed the initiative saying the CDS would help the market grow and discourage the kerb market.
Brokers said hundreds of retail investors had helped spur a surge in kerb market stock trading.
"They just trade securities by showing share certificates in the street outside the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) on payment of cash," one broker said.
DSE councillor broker Abdul Huq Howlader said: "There is no way to trade securities outside the DSE floor. The CDS is needed to check authenticity of share certificates."
But Howlader, who is one of the members of the committee on setting up the CDS, expected only 60 percent of shares to enter the system over a period of five to six years.
The benchmark DSE index has soared over the past couple of months on what brokers have called speculative trading.
The index reached all-time high at 2,193.8 on Thursday.
It had soared earlier this month but dived soon after when investors started panic selling over an SEC warning against trading on 24 losing companies and transactions through the kerb market.

The index dropped in successive sessions from 2,097.33 on October 7 to 1,793.58 on October 14. The DSE on October 10 fixed share price movement within 10 percent of the previous day's rate to discourage wild trading and end the quoting of speculative prices.
The index was at 1,145.54 on August 1.
